title: Credit Cycles
subfield: Macro-Finance / Collateral Constraints and Business Cycles
datasets: None (theoretical paper; illustrative numerical simulation only)
research_question: In an economy where debt must be secured by durable, productive collateral, how large and how persistent are the responses of asset prices, investment and output to a small, temporary shock, and can the interaction between debt and collateral generate cycles on its own?
main_finding: Because the collateral asset's price capitalizes the entire expected future path of credit-constraint tightness, the dynamic multiplier on asset prices exceeds the static multiplier by a factor equal to the inverse of the net real interest rate; a temporary 1% shock generates land-price and output responses of comparable size to the shock, persisting roughly a decade, and lumpy investment can generate damped, multi-year predator-prey cycles between debt and landholding.
research_gaps: No priced credit risk: lenders are risk-neutral, so the model speaks to credit quantities, not credit spreads
No theory of who becomes credit-constrained or when
Mechanism not robust to hedging markets against the aggregate shock (Krishnamurthy 2003)
Purely deterministic, one-time shock; authors flag a fully stochastic extension as the 'pressing next step'
research_ideas: Solve a fully stochastic, globally-solved version of the model with recurring, anticipated shocks
Test the lumpy-investment build-up prediction against farm- or firm-level micro data
Endogenize the supply of hedging instruments to restore amplification and generate a priced credit spread
Cross-country test of the elasticity threshold separating cyclical from monotonic collateral dynamics
Horse race between collateral-constraint and heterogeneous-beliefs explanations of asset-price overshooting

title: The Financial Accelerator in a Quantitative Business Cycle Framework
subfield: Macro-Finance / Financial Frictions and Business Cycles
methods: Dynamic New Keynesian (Calvo Pricing) DSGE Simulation
datasets: None (theoretical/calibrated DSGE paper; illustrative simulation only)
research_question: In a dynamic general equilibrium model with costly-state-verification credit frictions between lenders and entrepreneurs, how does endogenous variation in the external finance premium amplify and propagate the effects of monetary and other aggregate shocks on investment and output, relative to a frictionless benchmark?
main_finding: Because the external finance premium moves inversely with entrepreneurial net worth, a small monetary tightening that lowers asset prices and net worth raises the premium, which further depresses investment and asset prices in a self-reinforcing financial accelerator loop; calibrated to US data (steady-state premium 200 basis points, leverage 2, default rate approximately 3%), the mechanism roughly doubles the peak output and investment response to a monetary shock and adds pronounced hump-shaped persistence relative to a model without credit frictions.
research_gaps: Idiosyncratic risk (sigma) is calibrated, not estimated, from limited default data
Model abstracts from aggregate-risk hedging markets that could undo the net-worth channel (Krishnamurthy 2003 critique)
Homogeneous entrepreneurs; no role for heterogeneous firm-level financial health
Partial-equilibrium debt contract nested in a linearized DSGE, so global/nonlinear dynamics near the participation constraint are untested
research_ideas: Estimate the idiosyncratic risk distribution directly from firm-level default and recovery data
Introduce heterogeneous firms differing in net worth to study the cross-sectional distribution of the accelerator effect
Add a hedging market for aggregate risk and test whether the accelerator survives (Krishnamurthy critique)
Embed a working-capital cost channel so the premium also affects the price-setting margin, not only investment
Compare accelerator amplification across countries with different corporate leverage and bankruptcy regimes
